definition: A structured conversation that tests a design against its requirements before it is expensive to change: a short design document with numbers, a timed walk through the Well-Architected pillars, a pre-mortem, and recorded outputs - ADRs, owned actions and a verdict of go, go with conditions or not yet. Weight it by risk and hold it early.
example: The partner API review took 60 minutes, produced four ADRs and three actions, and ended "go with conditions: per-partner identities first".

definition: The requirements about how well a system works rather than what it does - availability, RTO and RPO, latency, peak load, security and compliance, data residency, cost ceiling, operability - stated as numbers so a design can be tested against them. "Highly available" cannot be reviewed; "99.9% monthly with a one-hour RTO" can.
example: Checkout: 99.9% monthly, RTO one hour, RPO five minutes, p95 under 400 ms at 2,000 requests per second, EU data, under $6,000 a month.

definition: The deliberate spending of one quality to buy another - a second region buys reliability with cost and complexity, private endpoints buy security with operational effort, a cache buys speed with staleness. Good reviews make every significant trade-off explicit, agreed with the business where it matters, and recorded in an ADR.
example: Active-active was declined: it would triple cost to cut an RTO the board had agreed at one hour.

definition: A short exercise in a design review: imagine it is a year later and the system has failed badly, then list the reasons why. It surfaces risks people hesitate to raise, and each credible one becomes a design change, an action or an accepted risk in an ADR.
example: The pre-mortem on the staff assistant produced "HR documents leaked to all staff", which led to group-based filtering in the index.

definition: The future cost of a shortcut taken now - deliberately, such as launching in one region, or accidentally, through neglect. Deliberate debt is recorded in a register with its interest (the ongoing cost or risk) and the trigger that forces repayment, so it is a decision rather than a surprise.
example: "Single region for launch; repay when revenue passes £2m a month or the board lowers the RTO" sits in the loyalty programme's register.
